title: Interoperable Legal AI for Access to Justice
author: Drew Simshaw

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Online disputes: Faster processing may not improve justice
st.an: The source does not evaluate whether faster online processing produces fairer substantive outcomes. Instead, it shifts the priority toward court-data standards, interoperability and institutional coordination as prerequisites for legal AI, while acknowledging that current infrastructure is limited and local implementation remains difficult.
qs: As AI on a broader scale continues to make inroads into other parts of life, courts still lag behind, and the public is likely to expect more from the courts in the years to come.53 One major challenge for courts is spearheading AI efforts on a local level.

st.t: Self-representation: Cheaper filings may shift institutional costs
st.an: The source does not assess whether GenAI caused rising federal self-representation, improved litigant outcomes, or shifted screening costs to courts and opponents. Instead, it redirects attention to fragmented regulation and technology, proposing a national sandbox to test and standardize interoperable legal AI. Its access-to-justice benefits are presented as potential rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: It will therefore be important to analyze the prospect of interoperable legal AI within broader discussions of legal-regulatory reform, including my proposal for a national legal regulatory “sandbox”—a reform mechanism that would provide temporary safe harbors for testing innovative services and collecting data in areas of regulatory uncertainty.

The proposed sandbox would promote standardization, transparency, and, ultimately, the technological and procedural interoperability necessary for AI to reach its potential as a tool to help close the access-to-justice gap and facilitate fair outcomes.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The excerpt is consistent with parts of the cluster: it identifies a fabricated-case sanctions incident, reports possible legal-AI capabilities, and raises an access-to-justice concern. But it is only a set of supporting citations and does not take a discernible position on the cluster’s principal proposition of human accountability, broad verification, or AI-specific disclosure and restrictions.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The source supplies contextual claims about AI-enabled efficiency, discovery-related displacement, sanctions from fabricated authorities, and access-to-justice regulation. However, it does not develop a position on the cluster’s central proposition that legal AI should remain supervised and tool-specifically verified, or on whether verification burdens consume efficiency gains; it also does not address lifecycle confidentiality controls.

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: Simshaw accepts that isolated, cheaper AI assistance across self-help, providers or courts is insufficient to close the justice gap. He materially extends the cluster by proposing coordinated technological and procedural interoperability, led by courts, as the institutional strategy needed to turn assistance into meaningful access.
qs: The time has come to appreciate that, although progress on all three fronts is necessary for closing the justice gap and maximizing fairness, it is insufficient if there is not also some level of shared commitment and coordination across—and not just within—all fronts.
Further, although the consumer and legal-services fronts remain critically important, courts should be recognized as the necessary drivers in achieving this interoperable legal AI.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source accepts the need for institution-wide judicial AI governance and materially develops it through Brazil’s experience: fragmented court projects prompted proposals for collaborative oversight, standardisation, interoperability, expert coordination and cross-sector partnerships. It supports lifecycle governance as a recommendation and cautionary lesson, while not demonstrating implementation outcomes or addressing verification, confidentiality and security in detail.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s concern that human assistance and safeguards may remain important yet unequally available, and materially extends it by identifying two concurrent risks: inferior technology-only assistance for low-income users and unequal distribution of powerful legal AI. It further adds design bias and concentrated power as reasons oversight must include coordinated, interdisciplinary governance rather than mere human accountability.
qs: Without large-scale coordinated efforts across all three fronts to level the playing field and facilitate necessary interdisciplinary and cross-industry collaborations, legal AI risks consolidating power, automating bias, and magnifying inequality.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts that AI can expand access while worsening inequality, overloading courts and failing to ensure fair remedies. It materially extends the cluster by making court-led interoperability, shared procedural and technical standards, and a national regulatory sandbox conditions for scalable, equitable deployment.
qs: It will therefore be important to analyze the prospect of interoperable legal AI within broader discussions of legal-regulatory reform, including my proposal for a national legal regulatory “sandbox”—a reform mechanism that would provide temporary safe harbors for testing innovative services and collecting data in areas of regulatory uncertainty.

st.t: Justice gap: Fair resolution exceeds legal assistance
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s broad framing by citing extensive unmet civil legal need and treating fairness as more than the provision of individual legal assistance. It materially extends the proposition by arguing that justice also requires visible societal standards, while presenting technology-enabled lawyer capacity only as a potential pathway rather than demonstrated effectiveness.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s central tension between expanding affordable legal help and maintaining protection, then materially develops it by identifying fragmented UPL and ownership rules as barriers to self-help innovation and by showing that legal-AI investment is concentrated in large corporate firms rather than access-to-justice settings. It also tempers its claimed benefits with misuse, technical-limit and bias concerns.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that legal AI offers bounded efficiency and access benefits but carries serious risks from technical limits, misuse, bias and unequal deployment. It materially extends the synthesis by identifying fragmented professional regulation and interoperable, machine-processable legal data as prerequisites for equitable adoption, particularly in access-to-justice settings.
qs: Without large-scale coordinated efforts across all three fronts to level the playing field and facilitate necessary interdisciplinary and cross-industry collaborations, legal AI risks consolidating power, automating bias, and magnifying inequality.

st.t: Regulatory sandboxes: Conditional entry tests consumer risk
st.an: The source accepts supervised sandbox experimentation as a way to test innovative legal services and collect evidence under regulatory uncertainty. It materially extends the cluster by proposing a national sandbox specifically designed to foster standardisation and interoperability, while presenting access-to-justice benefits as prospective rather than proven.
qs: It will therefore be important to analyze the prospect of interoperable legal AI within broader discussions of legal-regulatory reform, including my proposal for a national legal regulatory “sandbox”—a reform mechanism that would provide temporary safe harbors for testing innovative services and collecting data in areas of regulatory uncertainty.

The proposed sandbox would promote standardization, transparency, and, ultimately, the technological and procedural interoperability necessary for AI to reach its potential as a tool to help close the access-to-justice gap and facilitate fair outcomes.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that AI’s benefits are conditional on coordinated institutional redesign rather than tool adoption alone, and materially extends the cluster by proposing court-led interoperability across consumer tools, legal-service providers and courts. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that greater access or efficiency does not itself establish fair access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Further, although the consumer and legal-services fronts remain critically important, courts should be recognized as the necessary drivers in achieving this interoperable legal AI.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s claim that AI-enabled delivery depends on resources and operating capability, adding that large firms may have an adoption advantage through greater financial capacity, dedicated IT personnel or consultants, and access to tailored services. It does not address workflow unbundling, pricing reform, junior training or verification.

st.t: Judicial reform: Human oversight may become merely formal
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s interoperability and inclusion agenda, presenting shared infrastructure, coordinated governance and socially informed design as necessary beyond mere digitisation. It also cautions that local variation, funding and cross-country differences limit implementation. However, it does not directly examine whether human judicial oversight becomes merely formal under high-volume AI-assisted adjudication.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s institutional-absorption thesis by arguing that legal-AI integration depends on financial resources, technical expertise and access to tailored services. Its evidence is narrow, however, and does not directly address bounded automation, hybrid pricing, buyer-side reallocation or the continuing role of lawyers.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports the proposition that AI can improve task-level efficiency while substituting for some legal work and reshaping staffing and billing, specifically in discovery. Its displacement and productivity assertions are cited commentary without measurements or independent evidence, so they illustrate the cluster’s mechanisms rather than establish broader employment effects.

kp.k: Justice-gap progress requires coordination across three interdependent fronts
kp.d: Simshaw argues that consumer self-help, legal-service providers and courts must advance together: improvements within any one front can be frustrated by inaccessible tools or incompatible procedures elsewhere. This is a policy argument about conditions for effective AI deployment, not a measured finding that interoperability has closed the justice gap.
qs: The time has come to appreciate that, although progress on all three fronts is necessary for closing the justice gap and maximizing fairness, it will be insufficient if there is not also some level of shared commitment and coordination across—and not just within—all fronts.
The inverse is true as well—progress in the courts will be meaningless if lawyers or litigants are unable to access or use AI tools effectively.

kp.k: Persistent unmet need motivates systemic rather than local reform
kp.d: The essay cites the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 finding that low-income Americans receive insufficient or no help for 92% of substantial civil legal problems. Simshaw characterizes existing legal-technology initiatives as too local and limited to achieve nationwide impact, while also identifying overworked public defenders, underresourced courts and criminal-case backlogs.
qs: Low-income Americans do not get any or enough legal help for 92% of their substantial civil legal problems.
But the results have been too local, are limited in scope, and lack the scalability needed to maximize impact.

kp.k: Consumer tools enable self-help, triage and professional referrals
kp.d: Simshaw describes tools for routine documents, wills, prenuptial agreements and expungement, alongside tools identifying when professional assistance is appropriate. Illustrations include reported 2016 headlines that DoNotPay helped overturn 160,000 parking tickets and Rasa's AI-enabled expungement assistance in Utah. He qualifies these examples by noting regulatory uncertainty and DoNotPay's mixed reception, including awards and lawsuits; they are not comparative effectiveness findings.
qs: A service called DoNotPay, run by a then-undergraduate student at Stanford, made headlines in 2016 when it helped overturn 160,000 parking tickets.

Rasa, a technology-driven app-based service, helps people in Utah assess their eligibility for expungement of their criminal records and, if eligible, navigate the process with the help of AI-enabled software.
But AI can also help people determine when their case warrants professional assistance and can connect them with appropriate professionals when needed.

kp.k: Procedural fragmentation and professional restrictions constrain scalable innovation
kp.d: The essay identifies differing forms, filing processes and AI-use rules, jurisdiction-specific unauthorized-practice definitions, and restrictions on nonlawyer ownership as obstacles to cross-jurisdictional tools and lawyer–technologist collaboration. It cites ABA Model Rule 5.4(b) in discussing ownership restrictions, while locating actual regulation in individual jurisdictions. Simshaw regards current local reform efforts as insufficiently fast or extensive.
qs: Indeed, innovation in this space is stifled by uncertainty as to whether certain tools and services constitute the unauthorized practice of law, which is defined and regulated differently across U.S. jurisdictions.

In addition, partnerships between lawyers and technologists to develop and provide such tools are often hindered by the nearly universal prohibition in U.S. jurisdictions of nonlawyers holding any ownership interest in a partnership with licensed attorneys.

kp.k: AI investment disproportionately benefits large corporate law firms
kp.d: Simshaw identifies potential efficiencies in intake, eDiscovery, research, strategy and drafting, while acknowledging high-profile misuse. He argues that much development occurs within the largest corporate firms and that products such as Harvey AI target large firms. Reporting Bob Ambrogi's contrast between Legalweek and the Legal Services Corporation's technology conference, he emphasizes unequal funding and warns that tools may not transfer effectively to less-resourced providers.
qs: But much of this development is happening in-house at the largest corporate law firms.
While it is possible that such services will trickle down to benefit those outside large law firms, services designed for one setting do not always translate well to others.

funding gap between those who are developing legal technology to better meet the legal needs of low-income Americans and those who are developing legal tech to serve large law firms and corporate legal departments.

kp.k: Court digitization provides foundations but not comprehensive AI coordination
kp.d: The essay describes electronic filing, case management, online forms, kiosks and online dispute resolution as existing progress. It identifies the National Open Court Data Standards initiative, developed by the Conference of State Court Administrators and NCSC, as a useful but narrower foundation focused on collecting and cleansing data rather than analyzing it. Citing Coglianese and Ben Dor, it reports approximately 15,000 to 17,000 state and municipal courts and a lack of centralized national coordination of court technology.
qs: The initiative currently serves only to collect and cleanse data, not analyze or interpret it
According to the National Center for State Courts, approximately 15,000 to 17,000 different state and municipal courts exist in the United States

As such, there is no leadership or centralized national coordination among courts in the United States on the implementation of court-oriented technologies, which can be a major impediment to the adoption of novel technologies.

kp.k: Expanded self-help could intensify already strained court caseloads
kp.d: Simshaw predicts that scalable consumer and provider tools could generate additional cases that courts cannot absorb without their own changes. This is a prospective capacity concern rather than a measured AI-induced increase in filings. His broader argument also recognizes that AI-assisted problem solving and online dispute resolution could prevent some disputes from reaching court.
qs: To the extent that progress on the self-help and legal-services fronts continues, their limitations are likely to be further magnified if courts are not prepared for an increase in cases resulting from the rise of legal AI.
But courts already struggle to keep up with caseloads, and they are likely to struggle even more with any kind of increase, absent changes of their own.

kp.k: AI could reinforce inequality through opposite distributional mechanisms
kp.d: The essay warns both that low-income users might receive inferior technological substitutes when human assistance is appropriate and that highly effective AI might remain concentrated among wealthy clients and large firms. It also reports skepticism that AI will materially alter existing inequality. These are possible, nonexclusive outcomes, not demonstrated effects of a particular deployment.
qs: For example, if low-income individuals are relegated to technology-driven tools and services even when human-driven assistance would be more appropriate, it might be better than nothing, but still not as good as professional human services.
But the opposite could also be true: legal technology could become incredibly powerful and effective, but not evenly distributed.
These two-tiered systems of inequality are not mutually exclusive.

kp.k: Efficiency and uniform adoption do not establish fairness
kp.d: Simshaw warns that AI can automate bias through training material and designers' subjective choices, so access and efficiency alone are inadequate objectives. He reports that some form of risk-assessment formula or sentencing aid had been adopted in all but four states as recently as 2021, but explicitly declines to endorse these controversial tools as a model for interoperability.
qs: Access for access’s sake and efficiency for efficiency’s sake will not necessarily result in improvements to fairness, especially if AI is designed and implemented in ways that intentionally or unintentionally automate bias and magnify inequality.
As recently as 2021, some form of risk-assessment formula or aid in sentencing had been adopted in all but four states
this Essay does not argue that such efforts should be endorsed in moves toward interoperability.

kp.k: Interoperability requires five technical, institutional and social pillars
kp.d: Drawing on an existing cross-industry interoperability framework, Simshaw proposes technical compatibility and standards; organizational education, buy-in and aligned goals; compatible legal and public-policy arrangements; shared semantics; and attention to social values and conditions. He connects these pillars to open-source transparency, cross-sector collaboration, legal-regulatory reform and lawyers' access-to-justice responsibilities, including pro bono service and reasonable fees.
qs: Each of these pillars—technical interoperability, organizational interoperability, legal and public-policy interoperability, semantic interoperability, and socially informed interoperability—is discussed below.
For interoperability to flourish, there must be education, buy-in, and an alignment of goals across the ecosystem.
In courts specifically, the widespread and consistent use of open-source software could increase transparency into the judicial system and facilitate cross-sector collaboration.

kp.k: Shared legal data could improve tools and expose bias
kp.d: Simshaw recommends more consistently structured, machine-processable case law and integrated case data. He argues that these could improve self-help and professional tools, expand usable datasets and enable analysis of judicial fairness. The NSF-funded SCALES initiative illustrates efforts to address missing nationally linked information; the essay presents AI detection of judicial bias as a potential application rather than a reported study result.
qs: AI on the self-help and legal-services fronts could more effectively make use of case law if cases were more uniformly “machine-processable,” which would require ensuring consistency in structure and certain terminology before publication.
Such data, if effectively leveraged in AI-driven analysis, could be used to, among other things, detect bias in judicial decisions that might be difficult to detect absent the assistance of AI.

kp.k: Brazil illustrates coordinated infrastructure, with limits on transferability
kp.d: The essay reports Brazil's seventy-eight million lawsuit backlog in 2020 and initially uncoordinated judicial AI development. It describes the Electronic Judicial Process system and reports that by 2023 only about 1.1% of criminal, civil and administrative judicial cases remained paper-based. Simshaw treats this as a reference for shared infrastructure enabling AI, while expressly warning that institutional differences limit direct transplantation to the United States.
qs: In 2020, the Brazilian judicial system had a backlog of seventy-eight million lawsuits
By 2023, nearly all criminal, civil, and administrative judicial cases in Brazil were managed digitally, with only about 1.1% still paper-based, thanks to the deployment of PJe
To be sure, there are differences between the U.S. and Brazilian court systems, and what works for one country in regulating in light of legal technology will not necessarily work for another.

kp.k: Shared AI development could assist courts lacking technical teams
kp.d: Simshaw reports recommendations from the Columbia-affiliated Brazil Report for collaborative governance, open-source software, university and private-sector partnerships, a common AI-model platform and a national innovation laboratory. The proposed laboratory would pool datasets and expertise and share models and algorithms. These are reported institutional design proposals, distinct from the essay's evidence of actual digitization.
qs: From a technical standpoint, the Brazil plan envisioned embracing a common “factory for AI models” that allows “courts that do not have in-house technology teams to scale algorithms for their operations,” thereby facilitating “an open platform for AI development.”

From an organizational standpoint, the Brazil Report also called for a national “Laboratory for Innovation in the Electronic Judicial Process,” which would assemble national datasets to train tools, centralize AI expertise, and facilitate the sharing of information, including AI models and algorithms.

kp.k: Broader governance frameworks support safeguards and human intervention
kp.d: The essay uses the European Interoperability Framework to emphasize stakeholder engagement, cross-jurisdictional process alignment and user needs. It also invokes Biden's 2023 AI Executive Order as a governance reference for standardized evaluations and equity. Simshaw argues that interoperability would facilitate ethical principles including fundamental rights, equal treatment, security, transparency and user control, with humans able to intervene in individual algorithm-assisted decisions.
qs: robust, reliable, repeatable, and standardized evaluations of AI systems
such principles include respect for fundamental rights, equal treatment, data security, transparency, and AI under user control
has the ability to intervene

kp.k: National coordination could pool costs, expertise and evaluation data
kp.d: Simshaw argues that adopting a preexisting national framework would make investment less daunting for budget-constrained courts. Centralized interdisciplinary expertise could reduce duplicated troubleshooting, while consistent technology across courts could improve the quantity, quality and applicability of evaluation evidence. He positions a national legal regulatory sandbox, providing temporary safe harbors for testing services and collecting data, as a reform mechanism supporting this coordination.
qs: But investing in new technology would be much less daunting if a jurisdiction could adopt a preexisting national AI framework, as opposed to starting from scratch.
With interoperability, more courts could do the same thing with the same technology, improving both the quantity and quality of data collection and evaluation.
a reform mechanism that would provide temporary safe harbors for testing innovative services and collecting data in areas of regulatory uncertainty.

kp.k: Courts should lead incremental movement toward national interoperability
kp.d: Simshaw's central recommendation is court-led technological and procedural interoperability despite courts' traditionally reactive approach to technology. He does not provide a comprehensive US implementation roadmap: suggested starting points are compatible sandbox data collection and partnerships among early court-AI innovators, followed potentially by a national coordinating entity. Local resistance and intellectual-property issues remain acknowledged implementation concerns.
qs: It further argues that the courts must be the drivers of such efforts.
While it is beyond the scope of this Essay to present a comprehensive roadmap for such an undertaking in the United States, it is worth noting that interoperability can start small.
Eventually, a national entity could more realistically standardize such efforts on a larger scale, similar to the centralization envisioned in Brazil’s plan.
Of course, other issues will warrant attention along the way, including the intersection of interoperability and intellectual property.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Simshaw argues that AI can expand legal self-help, increase providers’ capacity and improve court processes, but nationwide access-to-justice gains require coordination across all three fronts.
pts.d: In this March 2025 essay, Drew Simshaw presents AI as potentially helping consumers identify and resolve legal problems or obtain referrals, enabling professionals to serve more people, and streamlining courts. His central conditional prediction is that isolated advances will not meaningfully close the nationwide justice gap without technological and procedural interoperability. He argues that courts must drive this coordination; this is a proposed institutional approach, not a reported nationwide outcome.

pts.k: AI is already supporting self-help and professional tasks, but jurisdictional fragmentation limits development and deployment.
pts.d: Simshaw describes consumer tools for routine documents, expungement eligibility and navigation, and professional referrals. For lawyers, he identifies efficiency gains in intake, eDiscovery, research, strategy and drafting, while acknowledging high-profile misuse. He argues that inconsistent forms, filing procedures, AI policies and unauthorized-practice rules inhibit scalable self-help tools. Ownership restrictions also hinder lawyer–technologist partnerships; the essay cites ABA Model Rule 5.4 and jurisdictional restrictions rather than treating the Model Rule as itself universally binding state law.

pts.k: Simshaw predicts unequal AI benefits across legal-market segments and warns that AI could entrench wealth-based disparities.
pts.d: Simshaw characterizes major generative-AI developments, including Harvey AI, as primarily designed for large firms. He cautions that tools developed for those settings may not translate to smaller practices or access-to-justice work. He identifies two compatible risks: low-income users could receive inadequate technology-only assistance where human help is appropriate, while wealthy clients could obtain powerful AI-enhanced professional services unavailable to others. He does not predict wholesale replacement of lawyers or quantify employment effects.

pts.k: Expanded AI-enabled access may increase court workloads, making court readiness a constraint on the benefits of legal AI.
pts.d: Simshaw predicts that scalable self-help and provider tools could bring more cases into already burdened courts. Without corresponding court reform, their benefits will be limited. He also recognizes a different pathway: technology-assisted problem solving and online dispute resolution can prevent some disputes from reaching litigation. These are conditional pathways, not a quantified net forecast of case volumes.

pts.k: Interoperability could improve AI effectiveness, affordability, transparency, bias detection and the economics of court adoption.
pts.d: Simshaw proposes technical, organizational, legal/public-policy, semantic and socially informed interoperability. Common standards, machine-processable decisions and integrated datasets would support AI use and analysis of judicial fairness. Shared frameworks and centralized expertise would reduce the burden of separate local development and improve data collection and evaluation. He also proposes a national regulatory sandbox to test services under temporary safe harbors and collect evidence about consumer protection and justice-gap effects. These are anticipated mechanisms and benefits rather than measured US results.

pts.k: AI-enabled efficiency and access do not necessarily produce fairness; poorly coordinated or designed systems may automate bias and magnify inequality.
pts.d: Simshaw distinguishes access and efficiency from fair outcomes. He identifies risks arising from toxic training material and subjective design choices, with particular concern about government AI. He argues that interoperability can support ethical principles including equal treatment, transparency, security and human intervention. His discussion of widespread criminal-risk assessment adoption expressly does not endorse those tools as an interoperability model.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The essay supports its US claims with secondary research, reported service examples, institutional initiatives and scholarly argument, not original AI performance testing.
pts.d: For unmet need, Simshaw cites the Legal Services Corporation’s 2022 finding that low-income Americans receive no or insufficient help for 92% of substantial civil legal problems. For self-help, he cites reporting that DoNotPay helped overturn 160,000 parking tickets in 2016, LegalZoom’s reported reach, Rasa’s service description and HelloPrenup’s investment; he also notes DoNotPay litigation and mixed results. These examples include broader legal technology, not exclusively generative AI. Professional-efficiency claims draw on legal scholarship and practice reporting; a 2023 sanctions incident illustrates misuse rather than a measured hallucination rate. Market-disparity claims draw on Simshaw’s earlier scholarship, Harvey coverage and Bob Ambrogi’s conference comparison. Court-fragmentation claims rely on Coglianese and Ben Dor’s 2021 account, including an estimated 15,000–17,000 state and municipal courts. NODS demonstrates existing data-standardization activity, not deployed interoperable AI. These cited sources support Simshaw’s argument; they are not interviews conducted for the essay.

pts.k: Brazil provides the principal comparative case for feasibility, with reported digitization outcomes distinguished from proposed AI-governance benefits.
pts.d: Simshaw relies on the 2020 Columbia-led Brazil Report, a 2023 study of electronic judicial processes and Brazil’s National Council of Justice’s 2024 Justice 4.0 report. He reports a 78-million-lawsuit backlog in 2020 and only approximately 1.1% of cases remaining paper-based by 2023, attributing digitization to PJe deployment. The Brazil Report supplies proposed integration structures, shared AI development, centralized expertise and open-source collaboration. The European Interoperability Framework supplies an additional governance reference. The essay does not present a causal estimate of how much interoperability reduced backlogs or improved justice outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The essay combines observations through 2024 with open-ended predictions and an incremental reform agenda; it specifies no deadline for closing the justice gap.
pts.d: Writing in March 2025, Simshaw calls for prioritizing interoperability in the coming years. Benefits depend on coordination, court capacity, usable consumer access, shared standards, adequate resources, interdisciplinary expertise, stakeholder commitment and attention to bias and consumer protection. The national sandbox and eventual national coordinating entity remain proposals. He acknowledges US–Brazil institutional differences, resistance to replacing legacy systems, intellectual-property questions and the absence of a comprehensive implementation roadmap. The essay invokes the 2023 Biden executive order as a governance reference rather than reporting a completed court-governance program.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are underserved legal consumers, differently resourced providers, courts and the public that depends on fair adjudication.
pts.d: Low-income people and self-represented litigants may obtain information, documents, referrals and access to court, but face risks from inadequate technology-only assistance or biased tools. The essay covers both unmet civil legal need and criminal-system pressures, including public defenders, expungement applicants and people subject to risk assessment. Legal-aid providers, solos and small firms could expand capacity but lack the resources and relationships of large firms. Wealthy clients and corporate legal departments are comparatively positioned to benefit from tailored AI-enabled services. Courts and adjudicative agencies face possible workload increases and adoption costs, while shared infrastructure could improve their capacity. Technologists and service innovators face fragmented rules and partnership restrictions. Broader public interests include fairness, transparency and legal-system legitimacy.
